messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert had spent forty years in sales, a career built on an unshakable confidence and an easy charm. At seventy, he was a senior figure in his firm, the man who could close any deal with a firm handshake and a well-told story. That version of himself, however, felt like a character from a novel he’d once read. The man who now sat in the consulting room was a stranger to him. The change began eight months ago, on a Tuesday night. He was walking the last few blocks home from a client dinner when a young man stepped out of an alleyway. The assailant smelled sharply of whiskey and desperation. Robert, ever the negotiator, tried to de-escalate. He spoke calmly, reasonably, offering his wallet without resistance. He believed his calm demeanor would defuse the situation, but instead, it seemed to enrage the man, who threw him against a brick wall before taking his things. The physical injuries healed, but the memory of his own powerlessness, of his voice sounding thin and useless in the cold air, remained.

In the weeks that followed, Robert’s world began to shrink. The most immediate change was his route home from the office. The thought of walking down that particular street was enough to bring back the metallic taste of fear and the rough scrape of brick against his cheek. So, he began taking a ten-minute detour, a small adjustment that felt like a monumental defeat. This pattern of retreat soon spread. His work often involved dinners where alcohol flowed freely, but the scent of whiskey on a colleague’s breath one evening sent a wave of panic through him so intense he had to feign illness and leave. He started trying to push the thoughts away, to erect a mental wall against the memory, but the effort was exhausting. To cope, he found himself cultivating a kind of deliberate blankness, a way of numbing his feelings so that neither the fear nor the shame could fully land.

These moments of triggered fear did more than just disrupt his routine; they fundamentally altered his perception of himself. Each time an unwanted thought of the assault surfaced, or he caught a glimpse of a young man on the street who resembled his attacker, the same litany of self-recrimination would begin. He had come to believe there was something profoundly wrong with him, a deep-seated defect that had been exposed that night. A stronger man, a better man, would have reacted differently. This conviction that the event happened because of the way he acted—his failed attempt at calm negotiation—gnawed at him. He saw himself not as a victim, but as a fool. The confident salesperson was gone, replaced by this hesitant, frightened man he no longer recognised.

This crushing self-appraisal became its own engine for his distress. The more he ruminated on his perceived failings and personal defects, the more the traumatic memories were dredged up. His self-blame acted like a magnet for intrusive thoughts, pulling the events of that night into the forefront of his mind against his will. His attempts to suppress these images only made them more persistent. He’d be in the middle of a sales call and suddenly be back in the alley, the smell of whiskey seeming to fill the air. This vicious cycle—his negative beliefs fuelling the very triggers he was trying to avoid—left him feeling trapped. He saw the man who attacked him from across a supermarket aisle two months ago, and the immediate, reflexive fear he felt only confirmed his own narrative of weakness, sending him into a week-long spiral of avoidance and low mood.

His wife, Helen, saw the life draining out of him. The easy laughter was gone, replaced by long silences. He had become a ghost in his own home. He finally sought help after turning down a keynote speaking opportunity at a major industry conference, an honour he would have relished a year ago. The thought of standing in front of hundreds of people, feeling like an impostor, was unbearable. He told the therapist his greatest fear wasn't another attack, but the certainty that the capable, confident man he once was had been destroyed for good, and that this fragile, broken version was all that remained.
